questions.why: Compressing or skipping parts of the context saves compute but can lose information exact attention would keep.

questions.q: How does a Mixture-of-Experts model with 47B parameters run at roughly 13B cost per token?
options: It's quantised to a quarter of its size
A router sends each token to a few experts only
It skips half of its layers for every token it processes
It uses only half of its vocabulary at a time
questions.why: Compute follows the active parameters, but memory still has to hold all experts.

questions.q: How does a vision-language model 'see' an image?
options: It reads the image's file name and metadata
A vision encoder turns patches into tokens the LLM reads
It runs OCR and then reads only the text found in the image
It can't; it only describes images it was trained on
questions.why: Each image becomes many tokens, often hundreds or more, which costs context and compute.

questions.q: How does one sentence of 8 tokens become 8 training examples?
options: The sentence is copied 8 times into the dataset
Every position predicts its next token, all in one pass
Each word is treated as a separate document with its own label
It doesn't: one sentence is one example
questions.why: Next-token prediction makes every position a target, which is why pretraining is so data-efficient per sequence.

questions.q: Why is deduplication important for pretraining data?
options: Only to save disk space on the training cluster
Duplicates cause memorisation, waste compute, leak tests
Duplicates help, because they reinforce the high-quality text
Models can't read the same piece of text twice
questions.why: Removing near-duplicates improves quality per token and reduces regurgitation.

questions.q: By the Chinchilla scaling result, roughly how many training tokens per parameter is compute-optimal?
options: About 1
About 20
About 1,000
It doesn't matter
questions.why: Earlier models were undertrained. Chinchilla found model size and tokens should grow together, around 20 tokens per parameter.

questions.q: Why was a small model like Llama 3 8B trained on about 15 trillion tokens, far beyond 'compute-optimal'?
options: By mistake: the run was left going too long
Over-training a small model makes it better and cheaper to serve
Small models need much more data than large ones just to work at all
To test how many GPUs the cluster could use
questions.why: Compute-optimal minimises training cost; when inference dominates total cost, a smaller, longer-trained model wins.

questions.q: Why does training a 70B model with Adam in mixed precision need around a terabyte of memory?
options: The training dataset itself must sit in GPU memory
~16 bytes per parameter: weights, grads, FP32 copy, Adam
Activations alone take a terabyte at this model size
The vocabulary's embedding table is extremely large at this size
questions.why: 70B × 16 bytes ≈ 1.1 TB before activations, so the model is sharded across many GPUs with FSDP or ZeRO.

questions.q: What do ZeRO and FSDP do?
options: They compress the training data so that it takes up less GPU memory
They shard parameters, gradients and optimiser state
They lower the learning rate as training goes on
They skip the backward pass for frozen layers
questions.why: Each GPU holds only a slice and gathers the rest when needed, cutting memory per GPU.

questions.q: The loss spikes suddenly at step 40,000. Which is a standard response?
options: Ignore it; loss spikes always recover on their own
Roll back, skip bad batches or lower LR, add z-loss
Double the learning rate to push through the spike fast
Delete the optimiser state and keep training on
questions.why: Spikes often come from exploding logits or attention scores; stabilisers keep them bounded.

questions.q: In supervised fine-tuning for chat, why is the loss masked on the prompt tokens?
options: To save GPU memory during fine-tuning
So it learns to write replies, not to imitate user prompts
Because prompts are random text that carries no useful signal for training
It isn't masked: prompt tokens are always trained on
questions.why: Only the assistant's tokens are targets; the prompt is context.

questions.q: How can a reward that isn't differentiable, such as 'the answer is correct', still train an LLM?
options: It can't: rewards must be differentiable to train with gradient descent
Policy gradients raise the probability of high-reward outputs
By turning the reward into a label for supervised training
By backpropagating through the grader's code
questions.why: You only need the log-probability of what was sampled; a baseline reduces the variance of the updates.

questions.q: What goes wrong if you optimise a learned reward model too hard?
options: Nothing: a higher reward score always means better answers
The policy exploits the reward model's blind spots
Training stops early because rewards stop changing
The reward model improves along with the policy
questions.why: A KL penalty to the reference model and early stopping limit this over-optimisation.

questions.q: How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO?
options: It uses more models, adding a critic network on top of standard RLHF
It trains on preference pairs directly, no reward model
It needs no preference data of any kind
It only works for image generation models
questions.why: DPO's loss implicitly defines the reward, which makes training simpler and more stable.

questions.q: In GRPO, used to train reasoning models, what replaces a learned value (critic) model?
options: Human ratings of each sampled answer
Each answer's reward relative to its group's mean
A second LLM that predicts each answer's expected value
No baseline at all: raw rewards are used directly
questions.why: The group mean acts as the baseline, which saves training a critic.

questions.q: What does distillation mean for LLMs?
options: Removing some layers from a model at random
Training a small model on a big model's outputs
Compressing the training dataset so that it takes less space
Quantising the weights to fewer bits each
questions.why: Learning from a strong teacher's traces can beat training the small model with RL on its own.

questions.q: How does LoRA make fine-tuning cheap?
options: It trains every weight in the model, but in 8-bit precision
It freezes the base and trains small low-rank matrices
It removes layers that don't change during training
It skips the backward pass for most layers
questions.why: Only a tiny fraction of parameters train. QLoRA also keeps the frozen base in 4-bit to fit on one GPU.

questions.q: Why do jailbreaks still work on safety-trained models?
options: Safety training is never applied to released models
Refusal training misses some phrasings, like role-play or codes
Models are simply unable to refuse any request they're given
Jailbreaks change the model's weights at runtime
questions.why: Defence needs several layers: training, input and output filters, and limiting what the model can do.

questions.q: What does raising the sampling temperature do?
options: It makes outputs shorter and more focused on the likeliest words
It flattens the distribution; rare tokens appear more
It removes all randomness from sampling
It changes the model's weights for that request
questions.why: Logits are divided by T before the softmax: higher T means more diverse and riskier text.

questions.q: How does min-p sampling choose which tokens to keep?
options: The k tokens with the highest probability
Tokens above a fraction of the top token's probability
Tokens until their probabilities add up to p, in order of likelihood
Only the single most likely token
questions.why: The cut-off adapts to how confident the model is, unlike a fixed top-k or top-p.

questions.q: Why does chain-of-thought prompting help on multi-step maths problems?
options: It makes the model larger for that question
Writing steps gives it room to compute before answering
It lets the model search the web for the answer while it writes
It lowers the temperature automatically
questions.why: Each generated step becomes context for the next, so hard problems are broken into easier ones.

questions.q: Why do LLMs hallucinate with confidence?
options: They are lazy and choose the easiest answer
Training rewards a plausible guess over 'I don't know'
They read the internet live while answering and repeat its errors
Temperature is always set too high
questions.why: Ground answers in sources, allow abstaining, and measure it, rather than relying on the model to know its limits.

questions.q: A new model scores suspiciously high on a public benchmark. What should you suspect?
options: Nothing: it's simply a much better model overall
Contamination: test questions were in its training data
The benchmark is too hard for the other models tested
It was evaluated on faster GPUs than the other models
questions.why: Use held-out or freshly written test sets and check small score gaps for statistical noise.

questions.q: Roughly how many FLOPs does it take to train a model with N parameters on D tokens?
options: About N + D operations
About 6 · N · D
About N² · D operations
About D / N operations
questions.why: About 2ND for the forward pass and 4ND for the backward pass is the standard back-of-the-envelope estimate.

questions.q: What makes operating LLM apps different from classic ML ops?
options: Nothing: it's exactly the same as classic ML ops
Prompts, models and data all change it; outputs need evals
LLMs never change once they're deployed
There are no deployments to manage, only API calls to outside vendors
questions.why: Version prompts and configs like code, and test changes against evaluation sets.

questions.q: Users say the assistant 'got worse this week', but all dashboards are green. What should you have been recording?
options: CPU usage on the servers
Full traces plus quality signals like evals and feedback
Only the error rates and status codes returned by each endpoint
Nothing; 'worse' is too subjective to measure
questions.why: Uptime and latency can be fine while answers degrade; you need traces to find what changed.

questions.q: Your provider retires your model in 60 days, and the replacement scores higher on benchmarks. How do you migrate safely?
options: Switch on day 59, when the old model stops
Run your own evals, adjust prompts, roll out gradually
Trust the higher benchmark scores and switch at once
Keep using the old model after it's retired
questions.why: Public benchmarks don't measure your task; your evals and a staged rollout do.

questions.q: Why can't input filters alone stop prompt injection?
options: Filters are too slow to run on every request at production scale
Attacks vary endlessly, so limit what the model can do
Prompt injection isn't a real risk in practice
Filters would block all normal text as well
questions.why: Treat model output as untrusted, give tools least privilege, and require approval for risky actions.

questions.q: Which approach typically cuts an LLM bill the most without losing quality?
options: Always use the biggest model to avoid retries
Route easy requests to small models, cache, batch
Raise max tokens, so each answer comes back in one call
Turn off logging and tracing to save on storage
questions.why: Most traffic doesn't need the strongest model; routing and caching remove most of the cost.

questions.q: Your LLM provider returns overload errors at peak time, and your retries make it worse. What should the client do?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop
Back off with jitter, respect Retry-After, cap retries
Send every request twice to improve the odds
Switch off timeouts, so each call can wait for as long as needed
questions.why: Synchronised instant retries create a retry storm; spreading and limiting them lets the service recover.

questions.q: A RAG app keeps citing an outdated policy page that was updated last week. Where is the likely problem?
options: The LLM's training data contains the old policy
The index wasn't refreshed, so old chunks are retrieved
The temperature is set too high for questions about company policy
The UI is caching an old answer
questions.why: Incidents like stale citations point at the data pipeline, not the model.

questions.q: Why can removing stop words hurt a sentiment model?
options: It makes each review longer and noisier, so it's harder to classify
Stop-word lists include 'not', which flips the meaning
Stop words carry most of the sentiment in a review
It doesn't: stop words never affect sentiment
questions.why: 'Not good' becomes 'good'. Preprocessing choices should be tested against the task.

questions.q: What does TF-IDF do that raw word counts don't?
options: It removes all common words from the text
It down-weights words found in many documents
It uses the order of words in each document
It learns a dense embedding for each word in a vocabulary
questions.why: A word like 'the' appears everywhere and gets a low IDF; a rare, specific word gets a high one.

questions.q: Why does a unigram model misread 'not good', and what fixes it?
options: It can't read short text; use longer reviews
It sees 'not' and 'good' apart; bigrams join them
It needs stemming to match 'good' and 'goods'
It ignores adjectives, so 'good' is always dropped
questions.why: Bigrams keep local word order that changes meaning.

questions.q: What assumption does Naive Bayes make about words?
options: Words appear in a fixed order
Words are independent of each other given the class
All words are equally likely to appear in every class
Only nouns carry information about the class
questions.why: The assumption is wrong for language but makes the model fast and surprisingly strong on small data.

questions.q: How does LDA describe a collection of documents?
options: Each document gets exactly one topic label
Documents mix topics; topics are word distributions
Documents form a tree from general to specific topics
Each document becomes a short list of keywords
questions.why: It is unsupervised: you choose the number of topics, and it finds the word groups.

questions.q: What does perplexity measure for a language model?
options: The number of parameters in the model
How surprised it is by test text, per token
How fast it generates tokens on standard hardware
The size of its vocabulary
questions.why: Lower is better. Perplexity k is like choosing uniformly among k tokens at each step.

questions.q: How is the edit (Levenshtein) distance between two words computed?
options: By counting the letters the two words share
Fewest inserts, deletes and swaps, via dynamic programming
By comparing only the first and last letters
By the cosine distance between the two words' embedding vectors
questions.why: A table builds up the distance between every pair of prefixes.

questions.q: How does an LLM handle a word it has never seen?
options: It skips the word and carries on
Subword tokenisation splits it into known pieces
It always replaces the word with a single [UNK] token
It stops generating with an error
questions.why: BPE builds a vocabulary by merging frequent character pairs, so any word can be spelled with subwords.

questions.q: Why is named entity recognition scored with entity-level F1 rather than per-token accuracy?
options: It's faster to compute on large datasets with many sentences
Most tokens aren't entities; half-right spans are wrong
Tokens in NER datasets don't have labels
Accuracy can't be computed for sequences at all
questions.why: Token accuracy looks high just by predicting 'O' (outside) everywhere.

questions.q: What does the Viterbi algorithm find?
options: The most common word in the whole sentence
The single most likely label sequence for the sentence
The main topic of the document that the sentence came from
The edit distance between two misspelt words
questions.why: It's used in HMMs and CRFs to label every word at once rather than one at a time.

questions.q: How is BERT pretrained?
options: By predicting the next word, left to right
By predicting masked tokens from both sides
By translating sentences between languages
By classifying whole documents
questions.why: Masked language modelling gives bidirectional representations that adapt well to classification and tagging.

questions.q: Why can BLEU score a word salad above a correct paraphrase?
options: BLEU checks meaning, but word salads fool its checks
It counts n-gram overlap, so matching words can win
BLEU always prefers the shorter of two candidates
It can't: BLEU always ranks paraphrases higher
questions.why: Overlap metrics don't understand meaning; use them with care or alongside human or model-based judgements.

questions.q: y = f(g(x)). What does the chain rule give for dy/dx?
questions.why: Multiply the outer derivative, evaluated at the inner function, by the inner derivative. Backprop applies this layer by layer.

questions.q: Why does neural network training use reverse-mode automatic differentiation?
options: It's more accurate than forward mode for every model and every input
One backward pass gives the gradient for all parameters
Forward mode can't handle matrix operations at all
It needs no memory for intermediate results
questions.why: Reverse mode costs about one pass per output; with one scalar loss and many inputs, it's far cheaper than forward mode.

questions.q: Why does high curvature limit how large the learning rate can be?
options: It doesn't: curvature only affects the final accuracy
In sharply curved directions, big steps overshoot and diverge
High curvature slows the GPU down during training
High curvature means a flat loss surface, so the steps barely do anything
questions.why: A second-order Taylor view shows gradient descent is stable only if the step is below about 2 / (largest curvature).

questions.q: What does momentum add to gradient descent?
options: Random noise that helps escape local minima
A running average of gradients that damps zig-zags
A second, separate learning rate for each layer of the network
Exact second derivatives of the loss
questions.why: Like a ball rolling downhill, it builds speed along consistent slopes.

questions.q: What does Adam do differently from plain SGD?
options: It uses the full Hessian to choose step directions
It adapts each parameter's step using running averages
It skips the backward pass for most of the model's parameters
It uses one fixed step size for every parameter
questions.why: Parameters with large, noisy gradients get smaller steps, and rare ones get larger steps.

questions.q: Why isn't Newton's method used to train large neural networks?
options: It converges too slowly once it nears the minimum
Its Hessian has n² entries, too big to store and invert
It only works when the loss function is convex
It can't use gradients, only the loss values themselves
questions.why: With 10⁹ parameters the Hessian would have 10¹⁸ entries. Approximations like L-BFGS or Adam are used instead.

questions.q: What is special about a convex loss function?
options: It has many local minima to choose between
Any local minimum is global, so the start doesn't matter
It can't be minimised with gradient descent
It's always a straight line in every direction, so any step works
questions.why: Linear and logistic regression are convex; deep networks are not, so initialisation matters there.

questions.q: PCA finds the direction of maximum variance subject to the direction having length 1. What does the Lagrange multiplier method show?
options: The answer is random, so PCA picks one at random
The direction is a covariance eigenvector; λ is its eigenvalue
PCA needs labels to choose between directions
The constraint can be ignored entirely without changing the final answer
questions.why: Setting the gradient of variance minus λ(‖w‖² − 1) to zero gives Σw = λw.

questions.q: An expectation you need is an integral with no closed form. What's the usual approach in ML?
options: Skip it and use the value at zero instead
Estimate it by sampling: average over random draws
Use only the single most likely value (the mode)
Set it to zero, since most such integrals cancel out
questions.why: Averages over samples converge to the integral; variational methods are another option.

questions.q: You encode a high-cardinality feature (e.g. 400 pincodes) by each pincode's average target value. What's the risk, and the fix?
options: None: target encoding is always safe to use
Leakage from each row's own label; compute it out-of-fold
Too many new columns: one for each of the 400 pincodes in the data
It only works for tree models, not linear ones
questions.why: Out-of-fold target encoding uses only other rows' labels, so the model can't read its own answer.

questions.q: Some values are missing, and whether a value is missing may itself mean something. What should you do?
options: Drop every row that has a missing value
Impute it and add a 'was missing' indicator
Fill it with zero and add nothing else
Remove the feature from the model entirely
questions.why: Missingness is often informative, like slow kitchens not reporting prep time; the indicator lets the model use it.

questions.q: Which model is largely unaffected by feature scaling?
options: k-nearest neighbours
Decision trees and tree ensembles
Logistic regression with L2 regularisation
Neural networks
questions.why: Trees split on thresholds, so rescaling a feature doesn't change the splits. Distance-based and gradient-trained models need scaling.

questions.q: You build a 'customer's average order value' feature to predict churn. How do you avoid leaking the future?
options: Use all of the customer's orders, past and future
Use only data available before the prediction time
Use the test set's averages so it matches evaluation
It can't leak, because it's only an average
questions.why: Point-in-time correct features match what the model will actually see in production.

questions.q: Where must feature selection happen when you cross-validate?
options: Once on the whole dataset, before cross-validation
Inside each training fold, as part of the pipeline
Only on the test set, after training
After choosing the final model
questions.why: Selecting features with all the labels first leaks validation information and inflates the score.

questions.q: Why does He initialisation scale weights by about √(2 / fan-in) for ReLU networks?
options: To make every initial weight positive and equal
To keep activation variance steady through ReLU layers
To speed up the GPU's matrix multiplications
To avoid needing dropout later on in training
questions.why: With the wrong scale, signals shrink to zero or blow up across 20 layers before training even starts.

questions.q: How do residual (skip) connections help very deep networks train?
options: They add extra parameters, so the network can fit more of the data
They give gradients a direct identity path backwards
They remove non-linearities from deep layers
They lower the learning rate for early layers
questions.why: Each block learns a change to its input, and the identity path stops gradients from vanishing.

questions.q: Why do Transformers use LayerNorm (or RMSNorm) instead of BatchNorm?
options: BatchNorm is newer and less tested than LayerNorm
Batch statistics are unreliable for sequences, small batches
LayerNorm has no learnable parameters to train
BatchNorm can't run efficiently on modern GPUs at all
questions.why: Per-token normalisation behaves the same in training and inference, whatever the batch.

questions.q: Why do LLM training runs warm up the learning rate at the start?
options: To save electricity at the very start of the run
Early Adam statistics are unreliable, so big steps blow up
To make the loss rise first, so that it falls faster later in the run
Warm-up isn't actually used in LLM training runs
questions.why: Ramping the learning rate up over the first steps, then decaying it, gives stable and strong training.

questions.q: You increase the batch size 8×. What should usually happen to the learning rate?
options: Keep it the same, since batch size doesn't affect it
Raise it roughly in proportion (linear scaling), with warm-up
Divide it by 8, so each update stays the same size
Set it to zero for the first thousand steps only
questions.why: Larger batches give less noisy gradients, so bigger steps are safe, up to a limit.

questions.q: How does dropout help a network generalise?
options: It makes the network bigger at test time
Dropping units stops co-adaptation, like an ensemble
It speeds up inference by skipping some units at test time
It removes the need for so much training data
questions.why: Activations are rescaled during training, so nothing changes at inference.

questions.q: Why is Adam with L2 regularisation not the same as AdamW?
options: They are exactly the same thing, just given different names by different libraries
In Adam, L2 goes through adaptive scaling; AdamW decays directly
AdamW doesn't apply any weight decay
L2 regularisation only works with SGD
questions.why: Decoupling weight decay from the gradient update makes regularisation behave as intended.

questions.q: What does mixup do?
options: It shuffles the labels between classes
It trains on blends of two examples and their labels
It mixes the training and test sets together
It averages the weights of several separately trained models
questions.why: Like other augmentation, it creates new training signal without collecting data.

questions.q: What does label smoothing change?
options: It removes the labels from noisy examples
Targets become slightly soft, like 0.9 instead of 1
It adds extra 'unsure' classes for uncertain examples
It averages predictions across several epochs
questions.why: Softer targets often improve calibration and generalisation.

questions.q: Your model can't overfit a batch of just 8 examples. What does that tell you?
options: You need much more data before it can fit
There's likely a bug: labels, loss, frozen weights or LR
The model is too big to fit so few examples without heavy regularisation
Training is working as expected for small batches
questions.why: Any working model should memorise 8 examples; failing to is a quick bug detector.

questions.q: Why does a 3×3 convolution suit images better than a dense layer?
options: It's always more accurate on every kind of data, not just images
It shares local weights across positions, so far fewer parameters
It ignores neighbouring pixels to avoid picking up noise
It only works on grayscale images with one channel
questions.why: Locality and weight sharing match how images work: an edge looks the same anywhere.

questions.q: Input 32×32, kernel 3×3, padding 1, stride 2. What is the output's height and width?
Before ResNet, why did much deeper plain networks get worse results, even on training data?
options: Overfitting the training data with too many layers
Harder optimisation: signals faded through many layers
Too little training data for such deep models to learn anything from
GPUs ran out of memory for deeper models
questions.why: Higher training error showed it was an optimisation problem; skip connections fixed it.

questions.q: What idea did VGG add to CNN design?
options: Skip connections around each block of layers
Stacking small 3×3 convolutions for a big receptive field
Attention layers between the convolution blocks
Depthwise separable convolutions to save compute
questions.why: Two 3×3 layers see a 5×5 area with fewer weights and an extra non-linearity.

questions.q: You have only a few hundred labelled images. What's the usual approach?
options: Train a CNN from scratch on the few images
Start pretrained, freeze most layers, fine-tune the head
Use a random forest on the raw pixels
Collect no more data and rely only on data augmentation
questions.why: Pretrained features transfer well, so small datasets can still reach good accuracy.

questions.q: How does a Vision Transformer (ViT) process an image?
options: It reads the image pixel by pixel with an RNN
It splits it into patches and runs a Transformer on them
It converts the image into a text caption first
It uses only convolutions, with no attention layers
questions.why: With less built-in image bias than a CNN, ViTs usually need more data or pretraining.

questions.q: How is an object detector usually evaluated?
options: Accuracy of the predicted class for each box
mAP, counting boxes right above an IoU threshold
RMSE between predicted and true box sizes
The number of boxes it finds in each image
questions.why: IoU decides whether a box matches; mAP summarises precision and recall across classes.

questions.q: Which architecture is a classic for image segmentation?
options: AlexNet, the first deep network to win ImageNet
U-Net, with skip connections for fine detail
A plain multi-layer perceptron on pixels
Word2Vec, trained on image captions
questions.why: The decoder upsamples to full resolution, and the skips bring back the edges lost by downsampling.

questions.q: How can a tiny, invisible change to an image fool a classifier?
options: It can't: classifiers simply ignore tiny changes
Tiny shifts towards higher loss add up across pixels
It changes the image size that the model sees
It removes colour information from the image
questions.why: Methods like FGSM use the gradient to find these adversarial examples.

questions.q: Why can't a plain RNN remember a word from 50 steps ago?
options: It has no memory of earlier steps at all
Gradients shrink as they pass back through each step
It reads every sentence backwards by default
Its vocabulary is too small to cover long, varied passages of text
questions.why: Backprop through time repeatedly multiplies by the same weights, so signals fade or explode.

questions.q: How does an LSTM keep information for hundreds of steps?
options: It has many more parameters than a plain RNN
Gates add to a cell state, so memory fades less
It never forgets anything it has ever seen
It uses attention over all the earlier steps
questions.why: The forget, input and output gates decide what to keep, add and expose; GRUs simplify this.

questions.q: What problem did attention (Bahdanau) fix in seq2seq translation?
options: Slow tokenisation of long input sentences
A single fixed vector for the whole source sentence
Translating between too many languages at once
Sentences that were too short to translate well
questions.why: Long sentences lost detail through the bottleneck; attention removed it, and later led to the Transformer.

questions.q: A model looks great offline but fails online. What is training/serving skew?
options: The model is too big for the serving hardware
Features computed differently in training and production
Users changed their behaviour overnight
The serving GPUs are slower than the ones used for training
questions.why: Computing features once, from shared definitions such as a feature store, keeps them consistent.

questions.q: When are batch (precomputed) predictions a good fit?
options: When each request needs fresh, live context
When predictions can be computed ahead of time
Never: batch predictions are always stale
Only for image models
questions.why: Batch is cheap and simple; online inference is for decisions that depend on live data.

questions.q: What is a canary deployment?
options: Running the new model on no live traffic at all
Sending a small share of traffic to the new model first
Deleting the old model once the new one is trained
Testing the new model offline only, on a held-out set from last month
questions.why: If metrics drop, you roll back with little impact. Shadow mode runs the model without serving its outputs.

questions.q: What does a model registry help you do?
options: Training models faster by using more GPUs
Tracking model versions with data and code
Labelling new training data automatically
Picking the best hyperparameters for you
questions.why: Without it, rebuilding last month's model or rolling back quickly is guesswork.

questions.q: Labels arrive weeks late. What can you monitor today to catch problems?
options: Nothing useful until the labels arrive
Drift in input features and predictions
Only the loss on the original training set
The size of the model file on disk
questions.why: Drift in inputs or outputs is an early warning, although not every drift hurts accuracy.

questions.q: How can you estimate a model's accuracy before any labels arrive?
options: You can't, until the labels arrive
Use its calibrated confidence scores to estimate it
Assume accuracy is unchanged since the day of training
Ask a sample of users whether it's right
questions.why: If probabilities are well calibrated, their average tells you the expected accuracy, a useful early check.

questions.q: What should stop a bad automatic retrain from reaching production?
options: Nothing; automatic retrains are always improvements
A gate comparing it with the current model first
Retraining more often so bad models don't last long
Using a bigger model architecture for every retrain
questions.why: Automated retraining needs automated checks, or a data problem ships straight to users.

questions.q: A recommender retrained weekly on its own clicks keeps showing the same few items. Why?
options: The model is too small to learn more items
It only learns from what it showed: a feedback loop
Users dislike variety, so they click less on new items
Clicks are random, so it can't learn
questions.why: Add some exploration or a randomised slice, and correct for exposure, to get unbiased training data.

questions.q: How does a recommender pick a few items for a user from millions?
options: Score every item in the catalogue with the full model
In stages: fast retrieval to hundreds, then a heavier ranker
Pick items at random, then learn from clicks
Show the most popular items to everyone, refreshed once every hour
questions.why: Scoring millions of items with a big model per request is too slow; retrieval then ranking keeps it fast.

questions.q: Why can interleaving compare two rankers with far fewer users than an A/B test?
options: It uses only offline data, so no live users are needed
Each user sees both rankers mixed; clicks pick a winner
It skips significance testing to save time
It tests one ranker at a time on all of the users
questions.why: Comparing within the same user removes between-user noise, so a preference shows up much sooner.

questions.q: You want to learn which image to show each user for each title. Why use a bandit rather than a fixed A/B test?
options: Bandits need no data to start choosing well
It shifts traffic to better images while learning
A/B tests can't compare more than two images
Bandits are always unbiased in the end, unlike A/B tests
questions.why: Keep a holdout or a proper test alongside it to prove the personalisation actually helps.

questions.q: Why keep the keyword index when adding embedding-based product search?
options: Embeddings are too slow to search at this scale
Embeddings blur exact tokens like model numbers; keywords keep filters
Keyword search is always more relevant than embeddings
Keeping both saves storage compared with embeddings alone
questions.why: Hybrid retrieval runs both and lets the re-ranker combine them; embeddings help most on long-tail queries.

questions.q: In a feed ranker, why combine several predicted actions in a value model instead of ranking by click probability?
options: It's faster to compute than a single click prediction
Clicks reward regretted clickbait; weighting actions fixes it
Click probability can't be predicted at all for brand-new posts with no history
Value models don't need any training data to work
questions.why: Multi-task predictions plus tunable weights let the product balance engagement types without retraining.

questions.q: You train a click model keeping only 2.5% of non-click examples. What must you do before using its predictions in the auction?
options: Nothing; the probabilities are already correct
Recalibrate with q = p / (p + (1 − p) / w)
Multiply every prediction by 40
Retrain the model on all the data
questions.why: Downsampling inflates predicted probabilities; the auction needs real click rates, so convert them back.

questions.q: A marketplace adds an embedding per listing to its ranking network. Training NDCG jumps, test NDCG doesn't. Why?
options: The embedding is too small to hold each listing's detail
Few bookings per listing, so its embedding memorises noise
Embeddings never work for ranking problems
The test set must contain different listings
questions.why: Item embeddings need many interactions per item, as with videos or words; scarce bookings make them overfit.

questions.q: Why does a notification bandit penalise templates a user saw recently?
options: To save money on sending each notification
Fresh messages work better; repeats get tuned out
Templates expire after a few days and must be rewritten
To keep the decision logs small and cheap
questions.why: A recency penalty with a half-life, plus softmax exploration, keeps messages varied while still favouring strong templates.

questions.q: In a short-video feed, why train the ranking model online on streaming actions instead of in a daily batch?
options: Batch training is impossible at scale
Interests and new videos change within minutes; online training picks them up, and beat batch by 14–18% AUC in the paper's live test
Online training needs no labels
It removes the need for retrieval
questions.why: Fast-moving feeds reward freshness; the reported live test showed a large AUC gain from training in real time.

questions.q: Why did the short-video system use a collisionless embedding table instead of hashing IDs into a fixed table?
options: Hashing is slower
Hashing makes different IDs share a row (7.73% of user IDs collided on a public dataset), which blurred them; collisionless tables did better
Collisionless tables use less memory always
Hashing can't handle new IDs
questions.why: Shared rows mix up the signals of different users or videos; the paper kept memory in check by admitting and expiring IDs instead.

questions.q: A job recommender upgrades its embedding model. Downstream models were trained on the old vectors. What keeps them working during the switch?
options: Retrain everything the same day
Learn a linear map from new vectors to the old space
Average old and new vectors
Keep both models forever
questions.why: A new model produces a different vector space; a learned map lets old consumers read new embeddings until they're retrained.

questions.q: Job matching is two-sided. Which measure reflects that?
options: Clicks on job posts only
Rewarding matches where recruiters respond (e.g. accepted messages) and capping how often one job is shown
Number of jobs posted
Time on page
questions.why: A match only works if both sides engage, and flooding a few postings hurts recruiters and job seekers alike.

questions.q: A food-delivery app launches groceries. Most new grocery users have long restaurant histories. What does the cold-start design do?
options: Show random groceries
Use an LLM to translate restaurant orders and searches into affinities over the grocery taxonomy, fed to the existing ranker as features
Replace the ranker with an LLM
Wait until each user has 20 grocery orders
questions.why: The LLM adds a signal the ranker was missing while the ranker stays fast and well understood.

questions.q: The LLM sometimes outputs grocery categories that don't exist. What's the fix?
options: Raise the temperature
Require exact taxonomy names, validate outputs and drop anything not in the taxonomy
Let the ranker learn to ignore them
Use a bigger model
questions.why: Validating against a closed list turns free text into reliable features.

questions.q: Why train one recommendation foundation model across many surfaces instead of separate models per surface?
options: It's always cheaper to serve
Each surface alone sees little data; a shared model learns from all of them and passes knowledge on to smaller models
Separate models can't use transformers
It removes the need for A/B tests
questions.why: Signals on one surface improve predictions on another; knowledge reaches surface models through distillation, representations or shared parameters.

questions.q: A foundation model is added as one retriever in an ensemble. How should it be trained to add the most value?
options: Copy the other retrievers' outputs
Find what the other retrievers miss, treating their predictions as hard negatives
Use only popular items
Train it on the ranker's scores
questions.why: An ensemble gains most from a member that covers different items, not one that repeats the others.

questions.q: Why do we randomly assign users to A and B?
options: To save money on running the experiment
So the change is the only systematic difference
To make each group smaller and faster
Randomisation isn't needed if groups are large
questions.why: Without randomisation, who gets the feature can be linked to the outcome, and the comparison stops being causal.

questions.q: What is a guardrail metric?
options: The main metric you're trying to improve
A metric that mustn't get worse, like latency
The number of users enrolled in the test
A metric you only look at once the test has ended
questions.why: Guardrails stop you shipping a win on one metric that quietly harms the business or users elsewhere.

questions.q: You want to detect an effect half as large as before, with the same power. How does the required sample size change?
options: It halves
It doubles
It roughly quadruples
It stays the same
questions.why: Sample size scales with 1 / (effect)². Halving the effect you want to detect needs about 4× the users.

questions.q: Your test is statistically significant. What else should you check before shipping?
options: Nothing more: significance alone means you should ship it now
Whether the effect is big enough to matter, plus guardrails
Only that the p-value is also below 0.01
Whether the test happened to start on a Monday
questions.why: Significant isn't the same as worthwhile; decide using the interval and the costs.

questions.q: You randomise by user but measure click-through rate per page view. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: CTR per page view is the standard metric
Views from one user correlate, so variance is understated
CTR can't be computed when users differ
The groups become unbalanced in size once some users view many more pages
questions.why: The analysis unit must respect the randomisation unit, or p-values come out too small.

questions.q: How does CUPED shorten an A/B test?
options: By peeking early and stopping sooner
By using pre-experiment behaviour to cut variance
By dropping the least active users, who add noise
By lowering the significance level to 10%
questions.why: Less variance means the same precision with fewer users, without biasing the estimate.

questions.q: Revenue per user is your main metric, and a few huge spenders swing every result. What's a common fix?
options: Drop the test and pick a different main metric
Cap extreme values or transform, then bootstrap
Only count users who spend small amounts
Use only the treatment group's median revenue
questions.why: Heavy tails inflate variance; capping trades a little bias for much more stable results.

questions.q: Your manager wants to check the test daily and stop as soon as it wins. How can that be valid?
options: It can't be made valid in any way
Use a sequential test built for repeated looks
Check only once a day, at the same fixed time
Use a lower p-value threshold just once
questions.why: Ordinary p-values assume one look; sequential methods keep the false-positive rate at 5% across looks.

questions.q: You tested 20 metrics and one came back significant at p < 0.05. Is it a real win?
options: Yes, definitely: p < 0.05 means a real effect
Not necessarily: about one false positive is expected
Only if the significant metric is revenue or similar
Yes, as long as the p-value is 0.049
questions.why: Use Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg, or treat the result as a hypothesis for a new test.

questions.q: You planned a 50/50 split but got 50,500 vs 49,500 users out of 100,000. Does it matter?
options: No: a 1% difference is well within normal noise
Yes: a sample ratio mismatch, likely a bug
Only if revenue also differs between the groups
Only for small tests with under 10,000 users
questions.why: χ² = 500²/50,000 × 2 = 10. Investigate before trusting any result.

questions.q: A new feature lifted engagement by 5% in week one. Why might it not last?
options: It always lasts once users have seen it
Novelty: interest at first can fade over time
Week one data is always wrong
Engagement can't change that fast, so week one is wrong
questions.why: Primacy effects run the other way: users resist change at first. Longer tests reveal the true long-term effect.

questions.q: A ride-app test showed treated riders booking 10% more, but after launch bookings barely moved. Why?
options: The test was too short to see the real, long-term effect of the change
Interference: treated riders took control riders' drivers
Riders gave false answers during the test
The launch had a bug that the test didn't have
questions.why: In shared markets, randomise by region or time slot (switchbacks) so the groups don't compete.

questions.q: When should you prefer a classic A/B test over a multi-armed bandit?
options: Never: bandits are always better
When you need a clean, unbiased effect estimate
When you want the most clicks during the test
When there are many variants to compare
questions.why: Bandits reduce the cost of showing worse options but give less reliable effect estimates.

questions.q: Your coupon test is flat overall. Could the coupon still be worth giving to some users?
options: No: a flat test means it helps nobody at all
Yes: uplift modelling finds who it changes
Only if you rerun exactly the same test again
Only for brand-new users who never bought before
questions.why: Average effects can hide positive and negative groups; validate any targeting rule in a new test.

questions.q: A new LLM tutor prompt looks better in demos. What's the right primary metric for a production test?
options: How good the demo conversations looked to the team
A real outcome like learning, with guardrails
The average length of the tutor's responses
The number of tokens used for each answer
questions.why: Demos are cherry-picked; randomise real users and measure what the product is for.

questions.q: AI-written email subject lines lost to the old rule-based ones. What's a sensible next step?
options: Ship them anyway, since AI models will improve
Find out why using segments and examples, then retest
Abandon AI-written subject lines for good
Run the same test again until the AI version wins
questions.why: A loss is information: find where and why it lost before deciding.

questions.q: A feed change affects what a user's friends see. How do you measure its real effect?
options: Randomise individual users as usual
Randomise clusters of connected users together
Ask users whether they noticed a change
Use only offline data from before the change
questions.why: Cluster (graph) randomisation keeps most interactions within one group.

questions.q: Why write the launch decision rule before the test starts?
options: It's a legal requirement for experiments
So results can't be reinterpreted after the fact
To make the test finish sooner, with analysis ready
It doesn't matter when it's written
questions.why: Deciding after seeing the data invites cherry-picking.

questions.q: What's a core part of a platform that runs hundreds of A/B tests at once?
options: Manual spreadsheets for tracking each test's results
Hash assignment, SRM checks, shared metrics, overlaps
Running only one test at a time across the company
A single dashboard showing total revenue every day
questions.why: Automation makes tests trustworthy and cheap enough to run many.

questions.q: Of all the lines that separate two classes, which does a support vector machine pick?
options: The first line the algorithm finds
The one with the widest margin to each class
The one through the origin, so it needs no bias term
A random line among the ones that work
questions.why: A wide margin generalises better; only the closest points, the support vectors, decide it.

questions.q: What does the kernel trick let an SVM do?
options: Train faster on data that's already linearly separable
Draw non-linear boundaries without building the space
Remove the margin so more points can fit inside it
Handle missing values in the features automatically
questions.why: Kernels such as the RBF kernel give curved boundaries at the cost of a linear model.

questions.q: When does k-nearest neighbours tend to fail?
options: With small datasets of only a few hundred rows
With many or unscaled features; slow to predict
When the classes are evenly balanced in the data
Never: it works equally well on any kind of data
questions.why: In high dimensions all points look roughly equally far apart. Scale features and reduce dimensions.

questions.q: Naive Bayes' independence assumption is almost always wrong. Why does it still classify well?
options: The independence assumption isn't actually wrong for text data
Classifying only needs the right class to score highest
It uses deep learning under the hood
It ignores the data and uses priors only
questions.why: Its probabilities are often over-confident, but the ranking of classes is frequently correct.

questions.q: What is the difference between LDA and QDA?
options: There's no real difference between them
LDA: one shared covariance; QDA: one per class
QDA is unsupervised, while LDA needs labels for training
LDA is built from decision trees
questions.why: QDA is more flexible but needs more data to estimate each covariance.

questions.q: What does k-means minimise?
options: The number of clusters that it ends up using
The squared distance from points to their centres
The distance between the cluster centres
The classification error against true labels
questions.why: It alternates assigning points to the nearest centre and moving centres to the mean, which suits round, similar-sized clusters.

questions.q: How can you choose k for k-means?
options: Always use 3 clusters, the usual default
Elbow, silhouette, and whether clusters make sense
Use the number of features in the data as the number of clusters
It doesn't matter: k-means picks k by itself
questions.why: No single rule is perfect; combine a metric with domain judgement.

questions.q: What does hierarchical clustering give you that k-means doesn't?
options: Much faster training on large data
A tree of nested groups you can cut at any level
Probabilities of each point belonging to each of the clusters
Labels for each cluster automatically
questions.why: The linkage method (single, complete, average, Ward) shapes the tree.

questions.q: Which clustering method finds curved clusters and labels points that belong to no cluster as noise?
options: k-means
DBSCAN
PCA
Linear regression
questions.why: DBSCAN grows clusters through dense regions, so shape is flexible and isolated points become noise.

questions.q: What does a Gaussian mixture model give that k-means doesn't?
options: Fewer clusters than k-means for the same data
Soft memberships and clusters with their own shapes
Much faster results on large datasets with millions of rows
Labels for brand-new classes
questions.why: It's fitted with EM and suits overlapping, tilted clusters.

questions.q: Why should you scale features before PCA?
options: PCA only works on integer-valued features
Otherwise large-unit features dominate variance
Scaling removes all the outliers in the data
It isn't needed: PCA handles any feature scale
questions.why: PCA follows variance, and raw variance depends on units.

questions.q: In a t-SNE or UMAP plot, what should you NOT read into?
options: Which points are close neighbours in the original space
The sizes of clusters and the gaps between them
That there are some groups in the data
The colours you used for each label
questions.why: These methods keep local neighbourhoods but distort global distances and densities.

questions.q: You have no fraud labels. How can an isolation forest flag unusual transactions?
options: It can't: anomaly detection needs labels
Odd points are isolated in fewer random splits
It clusters transactions by colour
It borrows fraud labels from similar companies instead
questions.why: Normal points need many splits to separate; rare, odd ones fall out quickly.

questions.q: Before trusting a fancy forecasting model, what should you compare it against?
options: Nothing: complex models always beat simple ones
A baseline like 'same as last week', on time splits
A random forecast, to measure how noisy the data is
The model's own error on its training data
questions.why: Many complex models fail to beat the naive forecast once tested honestly.

questions.q: What does it mean for a time series to be stationary, and how is a trend usually removed for ARIMA?
options: It never changes; by deleting the trend data
Its mean and variance stay stable; differencing
It has no noise; by smoothing the series
It's always seasonal; by averaging each season
questions.why: The 'I' in ARIMA is the differencing step that makes the series stationary before modelling.

questions.q: What does the entropy of a distribution measure?
options: The mean of the distribution
The average surprise, or bits needed per outcome
The largest single probability anywhere in the distribution
The variance of the distribution
questions.why: Entropy is −Σ p log p. A fair coin has 1 bit; a coin that always lands heads has 0.

questions.q: Why do classifiers train with cross-entropy?
options: It's always zero for a well-trained model
Minimising it maximises the true labels' likelihood
It ignores the wrong classes completely
It's faster to compute than plain accuracy on large batches
questions.why: Cross-entropy = entropy of the labels + KL from the labels to the model, so minimising it pushes the model's distribution towards the true one.

questions.q: Which statement about KL divergence is true?
options: It's symmetric: KL(P‖Q) equals KL(Q‖P)
It's zero only when they match, and isn't symmetric
It can be negative when Q is a much wider distribution than P
It's a true distance metric in the usual sense
questions.why: KL(P‖Q) and KL(Q‖P) generally differ, which is why which way you compute it matters.

questions.q: A language model's perplexity on test text is 20. What does that mean?
options: It got 20% of the next tokens exactly right
It's as unsure as picking among 20 equal tokens
It used 20 layers to make each prediction
It saw 20 tokens of context for each guess
questions.why: Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token; lower is better.

questions.q: What does entropy have to do with compression?
options: Nothing: they are unrelated ideas
Entropy is the lower limit on bits per symbol
Compression increases the entropy of data
Only images can be compressed using entropy
questions.why: A good model of the data predicts it well, and good prediction means fewer bits to encode it.

questions.q: When can mutual information find a relationship that correlation misses?
options: Never: correlation catches every relationship
For non-linear links, like y = x² around zero
Only for linear relationships
When both variables are constant
questions.why: Mutual information measures any dependence; correlation only measures linear association.

questions.q: Two distributions don't overlap at all. Which comparison still gives a useful, finite value that reflects how far apart they are?
options: KL divergence
Wasserstein distance
Jensen–Shannon divergence
Cosine similarity
questions.why: KL becomes infinite and Jensen–Shannon saturates without overlap; Wasserstein measures how far mass must move.

questions.q: A decision tree split reduces label entropy from 1.0 bit to 0.6 bits on average. What is the information gain?
options: 1.6 bits
0.4 bits
0.6 bits
It can't be computed
questions.why: Information gain is the drop in entropy: 1.0 − 0.6 = 0.4 bits.

questions.q: What does an embedding learn, for example for foods like biryani and pulao?
options: A random ID number for each item
A vector where similar items end up close together
The number of letters in each item's name
A single category label for each item, stored as a one-hot vector
questions.why: Embeddings place similar items near each other, so similarity can be measured with distances or cosine.

questions.q: What makes a variational autoencoder able to generate new data, unlike a plain autoencoder?
options: It has more layers than a plain autoencoder
A smooth latent space tied to a prior, for sampling
It uses class labels to guide the decoder
It skips the decoder when generating new data
questions.why: The KL term keeps the latent space well organised, so random samples decode into plausible outputs.

questions.q: Why are GANs hard to train?
options: They have no loss function at all for the optimiser to work on
Two competing networks can oscillate or collapse
They need labelled data for every image
They can't be trained on GPUs
questions.why: The generator and discriminator must stay balanced; tricks like better losses and normalisation help.

questions.q: How does a diffusion model generate an image?
options: It copies and blends training images
From pure noise, it removes a little noise each step
It draws the image pixel by pixel, row after row
It uses a GAN discriminator to pick images
questions.why: Training adds noise to real images and learns to undo it; generation runs that denoising many times.

questions.q: How did CLIP learn to match images and text without hand-labelled classes?
options: From manual labels for every image
Matching image–caption pairs scored above mismatches
By predicting the pixels of each image from the caption's words
By translating captions into other languages
questions.why: Contrastive learning pulls matching pairs together and pushes others apart, enabling zero-shot classification.

questions.q: In contrastive learning, what are the 'negatives'?
options: Examples with wrong labels in the dataset
Other examples in the batch that don't match
Images with negative pixel values
Training runs that failed to converge
questions.why: More and harder negatives usually make the learned representation more useful.

questions.q: Which family usually gives the most stable training and best image quality today, at the cost of slower generation?
options: GANs
Diffusion models
Plain autoencoders
Linear regression
questions.why: Diffusion trains stably and covers the data well; it needs many denoising steps, which faster samplers reduce.

questions.q: What is the intersection over union (IoU) of two 10×10 boxes that overlap in a 5×10 area?
options: About 0.5
About 0.33
About 0.25
Exactly 1.0
questions.why: Intersection 50, union 100 + 100 − 50 = 150, so IoU = 50 / 150 ≈ 0.33.
